title: Neural Tube Embryology and Its Malformations
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the central nervous system from a flat sheet of ectoderm to a closed tube, then to the vesicles that become the adult brain and ventricles, and to the three tissues that supply its cells. Each developmental step is paired with the malformation that follows when it fails: open neural tube defects when the neuropores do not close, holoprosencephaly when the forebrain does not divide, and the Chiari and Dandy-Walker malformations when the hindbrain and posterior fossa develop abnormally. Board questions give a screening result, a facial or skin finding, or an imaging description and ask you to name the step that failed. Timing, signals, and tissue of origin let you reason from finding to mechanism.
prerequisites: Gastrulation, the trilaminar germ disc, and formation of the notochord (week 3)
Gross organization of the brain: hemispheres, diencephalon, brainstem, cerebellum, and ventricles
Folate and one-carbon metabolism in thymidylate and purine synthesis
Meiotic nondisjunction and the autosomal trisomies
Basic signal transduction: ligands, receptors, and transcription factors

connections.how: The glial cells whose origins are set here (oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, Schwann cells, microglia) respond differently to injury because they come from different tissues.

connections.to: CNS blood supply and CSF flow (NE-10)
connections.how: The ventricles are the persistent lumen of the neural tube, so the CSF pathway follows the vesicles and explains where hydrocephalus begins.
Aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, and Dandy-Walker malformation are developmental causes of obstructive hydrocephalus.
Trisomy 13 and single-gene defects in the sonic hedgehog pathway are major causes of holoprosencephaly.
Hirschsprung disease is a failure of neural crest cells to colonize the distal colon, a direct consequence of crest migration described here.

The thickened strip of dorsal ectoderm (neuroectoderm) that forms over the notochord and folds into the neural tube.
The raised lateral edge of the neural plate; paired folds meet and fuse in the midline to close the tube.
Cells that detach from the crests of the neural folds during fusion and migrate to form peripheral neurons, glia, and many non-neural tissues.
One of the two open ends of the neural tube, cranial and caudal, which are the last parts of the tube to close.

The main fetal plasma protein, made by the yolk sac and fetal liver, which leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal blood from open neural tube defects.
A secreted, cholesterol-modified signaling protein that specifies ventral midline tissue in the neural tube, forebrain, and face.

A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, most often cervical and often associated with Chiari I malformation.

sections.title: Neurulation: induction, folding, fusion, and neuropore closure

blocks.text: Neurulation is the process by which ectoderm on the dorsal surface of the embryo becomes the neural tube, the precursor of the brain and spinal cord. It begins in week 3, while gastrulation is still adding mesoderm at the caudal end of the embryo, and the tube is closed by the end of week 4.

The notochord, a rod of axial mesoderm formed during gastrulation, and the prechordal mesoderm in front of it induce the overlying ectoderm to become neural. Ectoderm exposed to bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) becomes epidermis. The notochord and prechordal mesoderm secrete the BMP antagonists noggin, chordin, and follistatin, which bind BMP4 and keep it from its receptors, and ectoderm released from BMP signaling adopts its default neural fate. The result, at about day 18 to 19, is the neural plate: a thickened strip of pseudostratified neuroectoderm lying directly over the notochord and broader at its cranial end.

The lateral edges of the plate rise as neural folds, leaving the neural groove in the midline between them. Elevation is driven partly by the plate cells themselves, which constrict their apical surfaces with actin and myosin and become wedge shaped at hinge points, and partly by expansion of the adjacent mesoderm and surface ectoderm. The folds first meet and fuse in the future cervical region, at about the level of the fifth somite, around day 22. Fusion then proceeds both cranially and caudally. As the folds fuse, surface ectoderm separates from the tube and closes over it as future epidermis, and cells at the crests of the folds detach as neural crest.

blocks.title: Neurulation and neuropore closure
steps: Notochord secretes noggin, chordin, and follistatin
BMP4 blocked; ectoderm forms neural plate (about day 18 to 19)
Plate edges rise as neural folds around the neural groove
Folds fuse first in future cervical region (about day 22)
Fusion spreads cranially and caudally; neural crest detaches
Cranial neuropore closes about day 25
Caudal neuropore closes about day 28
blocks.caption: Fusion starts in the middle of the tube and spreads toward both ends, so the two neuropores are the last openings to seal and the commonest sites of failure.

blocks.text: Until fusion is complete, the two ends of the tube remain open to the amniotic cavity as the cranial (anterior) and caudal (posterior) neuropores. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 28. As the last sites to close, they are the commonest sites of failure: failed cranial closure produces anencephaly, and failed caudal closure produces lumbosacral myelomeningocele (C04). Once both close, the lumen is a sealed cavity that becomes the ventricles and the central canal. The lowest sacral and coccygeal cord segments form afterward by secondary neurulation, in which a solid mass of tail bud cells hollows out and joins the primary tube.

The closed tube is then patterned dorsoventrally. Sonic hedgehog (SHH) from the notochord and from the floor plate of the tube directs ventral cells to become motor neurons (basal plate), while BMPs from the roof plate and overlying ectoderm specify dorsal sensory neurons (alar plate). This is why motor nuclei lie ventral, or medial in the brainstem, and sensory nuclei lie dorsal, or lateral.

blocks.predict: A teratogen acts only on day 32 of development. Could it cause anencephaly or an open myelomeningocele?
blocks.explain: No. Both neuropores have closed by about day 28, and an open neural tube defect requires interference with closure itself. An insult after closure can damage the formed brain or cord but cannot reopen the tube.

sections.title: Brain vesicles, their adult derivatives, and the ventricles

blocks.text: By the end of week 4, as the cranial neuropore closes, the cranial end of the tube expands into three primary vesicles: the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). The caudal tube stays narrow and becomes the spinal cord. The tube also bends at three flexures: the cephalic flexure at the midbrain and the cervical flexure at the hindbrain and cord junction, both concave ventrally, and the pontine flexure between them, which bends the opposite way and spreads the thin roof of the hindbrain.

In week 5 two of the primary vesicles divide, giving five secondary vesicles. The prosencephalon divides into the telencephalon, whose paired lateral outgrowths become the cerebral hemispheres, and the diencephalon. The rhombencephalon divides into the metencephalon and myelencephalon. The mesencephalon does not divide. Each secondary vesicle produces a fixed set of adult structures.

blocks.title: Brain vesicles and their adult derivatives
rows: Cerebral cortex and white matter, caudate and putamen, hippocampus, amygdala, olfactory bulbs
Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus with pineal gland, retina and optic nerve, posterior pituitary
blocks.caption: The lumen of each vesicle persists as a ventricle, so the cavity identifies the vesicle of origin.

blocks.text: The lumen of the tube is never lost; it widens or narrows with the wall around it. The lateral ventricles are the cavities of the hemispheres and drain through the interventricular foramina (of Monro) into the third ventricle of the diencephalon. The walls of the mesencephalon thicken greatly, so its lumen narrows to the cerebral aqueduct, which joins the fourth ventricle of the rhombencephalon. The roof of the fourth ventricle, thinned by the pontine flexure, carries choroid plexus and later opens through the median and lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space. The aqueduct is the narrowest channel in the system, so aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus.

Several structures that seem separate from the brain are outgrowths of the diencephalon. The optic vesicle forms the retina and optic nerve, so the optic nerve is a CNS tract myelinated by oligodendrocytes and can be affected by multiple sclerosis. The infundibulum grows down from the diencephalic floor to form the posterior pituitary, and the pineal gland arises from its roof. The anterior pituitary, by contrast, comes from Rathke pouch, an outgrowth of oral ectoderm, not from the neural tube.

blocks.title: Localizing an obstruction by which ventricles are enlarged
blocks.text: A fetal MRI shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth ventricle. CSF is made mainly by the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles and flows through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and out through its apertures. Every space upstream of a block dilates and every space downstream does not. The lateral and third ventricles are enlarged, so the block lies beyond the third ventricle; the fourth is normal, so the block lies before it. The only channel between them is the aqueduct, the lumen of the mesencephalon, so this is aqueductal stenosis. If the fourth ventricle were also greatly dilated, the obstruction would lie at its outlet, as in Dandy-Walker malformation (C06).

sections.title: Neuroectoderm, neural crest, and mesoderm derivatives

blocks.text: The nervous system draws its cells from three sources, and the source of a cell predicts where it lives, how it behaves, and which diseases arise from it. Neuroectoderm is the wall of the neural tube itself. Neural crest is the population that detaches from the crests of the neural folds during fusion. Mesoderm contributes the microglia, the dura, and the blood vessels.

Neuroepithelial cells lining the tube divide in the ventricular zone and produce, first, neuroblasts, which become all CNS neurons, and later glioblasts, which become astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. Radial glia act both as progenitors and as scaffolds along which young neurons migrate outward to form the cortex. Cells that remain lining the lumen become ependyma, the ciliated epithelium of the ventricles and central canal, and specialized ependyma forms the epithelium of the choroid plexus. The retina, the glia of the optic nerve, the posterior pituitary, and the pineal gland are also neuroectoderm because they grow out of the tube (C02).

Neural crest cells undergo an epithelial to mesenchymal transition: they lose their E-cadherin junctions, become motile, and migrate along defined pathways. In the trunk they form the sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia, the postganglionic neurons of sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric ganglia, the Schwann cells and satellite cells of peripheral nerves and ganglia, the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, and melanocytes. In the head they also form much of the facial skeleton and connective tissue, sensory ganglia of several cranial nerves (with ectodermal placodes), odontoblasts, and, in cardiac crest, the aorticopulmonary septum. The adrenal medulla shows how origin explains function: chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons, so they receive preganglionic cholinergic fibers directly and release mainly epinephrine into the blood rather than onto a target organ.

Microglia are the exception among CNS glia. They derive from yolk sac macrophage progenitors (mesoderm) that colonize the brain early, so they belong to the mononuclear phagocyte lineage: they phagocytose debris, present antigen, and are the main CNS cells infected by HIV, fusing into multinucleated giant cells.

rows: CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma, choroid plexus epithelium, retina, posterior pituitary, pineal gland
Dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia, autonomic and enteric ganglia, Schwann and satellite cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, facial skeleton, odontoblasts, aorticopulmonary septum
Hirschsprung disease, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, melanoma, schwannoma
Microglia (yolk sac macrophage lineage), dura mater, CNS blood vessels
Multinucleated giant cells of HIV encephalitis (microglia)
Anterior pituitary (Rathke pouch), lens, epidermis, inner ear and olfactory epithelium (placodes)
blocks.caption: Cells that stay inside the brain and cord come from the tube; cells scattered in the periphery come from crest; microglia come from mesoderm.

blocks.text: The two myelinating cells show why origin matters clinically. Oligodendrocytes (neuroectoderm) each myelinate segments of many CNS axons and are the target in multiple sclerosis. Schwann cells (neural crest) each myelinate a single internode of one peripheral axon, support axon regeneration, are the target in Guillain-Barre syndrome, and give rise to schwannomas. Because crest cells migrate, disorders of crest migration or proliferation appear far from the neural tube: Hirschsprung disease when crest fails to reach the distal colon, neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma in the adrenal medulla, and melanoma in the skin.

blocks.predict: A child has an adrenal tumor that secretes catecholamines. Does it share a tissue of origin with an ependymoma of the fourth ventricle?
blocks.explain: No. Adrenal medullary tumors (neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma) arise from neural crest cells that migrated away from the tube, whereas ependymoma arises from neuroectoderm that stayed lining the lumen.
blocks.check: Compare with the neural crest and neuroectoderm rows of the cell origin table.

sections.title: Neural tube defects, alpha-fetoprotein, and folate

blocks.text: Neural tube defects result from failure of the tube to close, or from incomplete formation of its coverings. The closed tube induces the surrounding mesoderm to form the vertebral arches and skull vault, so an open tube leaves the bony covering incomplete. The defects are ranked by how much neural tissue is involved and whether skin covers it, which determines both the neurological outcome and the screening result.

blocks.title: Neural tube defects compared
rows: Unfused vertebral arch only, usually L5 or S1
Usually silent; hair tuft, dimple, or lipoma over the defect
Meninges and CSF; cord in place
Normal if skin covered; raised if open
Meninges plus cord or roots, usually lumbosacral
Deficits below the level, neurogenic bladder, Chiari II, hydrocephalus
No skull vault; exposed, degenerated forebrain
blocks.caption: Only defects exposing neural tissue to amniotic fluid raise AFP and AChE.

blocks.text: Myelomeningocele is the most common serious open defect and usually reflects failed closure of the caudal neuropore. The exposed cord and roots are further damaged by amniotic fluid, so function is lost below the level: lower motor neuron leg weakness, sensory loss, and neurogenic bladder and bowel from involvement of S2 to S4. Nearly every child with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele also has a Chiari II malformation, and most develop hydrocephalus (C06). Anencephaly is the cranial counterpart: the exposed forebrain degenerates, the skull vault does not form, and impaired fetal swallowing causes polyhydramnios.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the main fetal plasma protein, made by the yolk sac and then the fetal liver. Normally little reaches the amniotic fluid, mainly through fetal urine. In an open defect, fetal plasma leaks from exposed neural tissue and its vessels, raising amniotic AFP, and more AFP then crosses to the mother, raising maternal serum AFP (MSAFP), usually screened at about 15 to 20 weeks. Acetylcholinesterase (AChE), a neural enzyme not normally detectable in amniotic fluid, appears only when neural tissue is exposed, so it is more specific. Skin-covered lesions leave both values normal.

blocks.title: From folate deficiency to raised maternal serum AFP
steps: Low folate slows DNA synthesis in dividing neural folds
Caudal neuropore fails to close by about day 28
Vertebral arches cannot form over the open tube
Exposed neural tissue leaks AFP and acetylcholinesterase
Amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase rise
AFP crosses to the mother, raising maternal serum AFP
blocks.caption: Each step explains one finding.

blocks.text: Folate deficiency is the best established modifiable risk factor. Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units: N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate donates the carbon thymidylate synthase uses to make dTMP, and N10-formyl tetrahydrofolate supplies two carbons of the purine ring, so limited folate slows DNA synthesis in the rapidly dividing neural folds. Folate also remethylates homocysteine to methionine for DNA methylation, and raised maternal homocysteine and some MTHFR variants increase risk. Because the tube closes by day 28, the mother's folate status at conception is what counts, and periconceptional folic acid substantially lowers risk. Other risk factors are valproate (which interferes with folate metabolism and inhibits histone deacetylases), pregestational diabetes, obesity, and hyperthermia in early pregnancy.

blocks.title: Interpreting a raised maternal serum AFP
blocks.text: An MSAFP is reported as 2.8 multiples of the median (MoM). AFP rises through the second trimester, so each result is compared with the median for that gestational age; about 2.0 to 2.5 MoM is the usual cutoff. First ask whether the value is truly high: a pregnancy further along than recorded makes a normal value look raised, and twins double the fetal source. With both confirmed, the remaining causes are leaks of fetal plasma: an open neural tube defect, gastroschisis or omphalocele, or fetal death. Raised amniotic acetylcholinesterase points to exposed neural tissue. A low MSAFP is instead associated with trisomy 21 and 18.

sections.title: Holoprosencephaly, sonic hedgehog, and the midline face

blocks.text: Holoprosencephaly is failure of the prosencephalon to divide into two cerebral hemispheres with two lateral ventricles, a division that normally takes place at about weeks 5 to 6. It is a spectrum. In alobar holoprosencephaly there is a single midline ventricle, fused thalami, and no interhemispheric fissure or corpus callosum. In semilobar forms the posterior hemispheres are partly separated, and in lobar forms the hemispheres are largely separate, with fusion limited to the basal frontal region. Olfactory bulbs and tracts are often absent in severe forms.

The forebrain divides because its ventral midline is specified by signals from the prechordal plate, the mesoderm just cranial to the notochord. The key signal is sonic hedgehog (SHH). SHH binds its receptor Patched, which relieves Patched inhibition of Smoothened and activates GLI transcription factors that drive midline gene expression. The resulting midline tissue separates the single forebrain field into right and left halves. Loss of function anywhere along this pathway can produce holoprosencephaly: mutations in SHH itself or in other midline genes such as ZIC2 and SIX3, defective cholesterol synthesis, and teratogens. Cholesterol matters because SHH is covalently attached to cholesterol during its processing and Smoothened activity depends on sterols, so Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (7-dehydrocholesterol reductase deficiency) can cause holoprosencephaly. Cyclopamine, a plant alkaloid that blocks Smoothened, produces cyclopia in grazing animals.

blocks.title: Sonic hedgehog and division of the forebrain
steps: Prechordal plate and ventral forebrain secrete cholesterol-modified SHH
SHH binds Patched, releasing Smoothened to activate GLI
Midline tissue forms in the ventral forebrain and midface
Single eye field splits into two eye primordia
Prosencephalon divides into two telencephalic hemispheres
blocks.caption: Loss of any step (SHH, ZIC2, or SIX3 mutation, trisomy 13, defective cholesterol synthesis, or Smoothened blockade) leaves a single forebrain and a deficient midface.

blocks.text: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is the most common chromosomal cause, and holoprosencephaly is one of its characteristic features alongside microphthalmia, cleft lip and palate, postaxial polydactyly, scalp defects (cutis aplasia), congenital heart disease, and severe intellectual disability. Holoprosencephaly also occurs with other chromosome abnormalities, including trisomy 18, and is more common in infants of mothers with pregestational diabetes.

The face is involved because the same midline signal shapes the midface. Early on, a single eye field lies across the anterior neural plate, and SHH from the prechordal plate suppresses its midline portion so that two eyes form. The nasal septum, philtrum, and premaxilla develop from the medial nasal prominences, which also depend on midline signaling. With too little midline tissue the eyes lie close together (hypotelorism) or fuse into a single median eye (cyclopia, often with a proboscis above it), the nose may have a single nostril, the premaxilla is absent, giving a median cleft lip, and a single central maxillary incisor may be the only sign of the mildest form. Because brain and face share one signal, the severity of the facial defect usually parallels the severity of the brain defect. The common lateral cleft lip is different: it reflects failed fusion of the maxillary prominence with the merged medial nasal prominences and does not by itself imply holoprosencephaly.

sections.title: Chiari I, Chiari II, and Dandy-Walker malformations

blocks.text: The three posterior fossa malformations are defined by where the cerebellum lies relative to the foramen magnum, by fossa size, and by the effect on CSF flow.

blocks.title: Posterior fossa malformations compared
rows: Tonsils at least about 5 mm below the foramen magnum
Vermis absent or hypoplastic; no herniation
blocks.caption: Fossa size separates Dandy-Walker from both Chiari forms; the open spine and extra displaced structures separate Chiari II from Chiari I.

blocks.text: In Chiari I malformation the cerebellar tonsils extend at least about 5 mm below the foramen magnum, usually because the posterior fossa is too small for its contents (underdeveloped occipital bone, a paraxial mesoderm derivative). The brainstem and fourth ventricle stay in place, and there is no neural tube defect. It is often incidental or causes occipital headache worsened by coughing or straining, which raises intracranial pressure and pushes the tonsils down. Crowding at the foramen magnum impairs the normal pulsatile movement of CSF between cranial and spinal subarachnoid spaces, and the altered pressure waves are thought to drive fluid into the cord, forming a cervical syrinx (syringomyelia) in a substantial proportion of patients.

A cervical syrinx expands from the center of the cord. It first interrupts the pain and temperature fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure, giving bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape over the shoulders and arms while the dorsal columns, and therefore fine touch, vibration, and proprioception, are spared (dissociated sensory loss). As it enlarges it destroys anterior horn cells, causing lower motor neuron weakness and wasting of the hand muscles, and compresses the lateral corticospinal tracts, causing upper motor neuron signs in the legs.

Chiari II malformation is congenital and more severe. The posterior fossa is small, and the vermis, fourth ventricle, and medulla are displaced through the foramen magnum, with kinking of the medulla and beaking of the tectum. It occurs almost only with an open lumbosacral myelomeningocele, and the leading hypothesis links the two (flow below). Displaced tissue blocks outflow from the fourth ventricle, and aqueductal stenosis is common, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Stretch on the brainstem and lower cranial nerves explains neonatal stridor from vocal cord paresis, swallowing difficulty, and apnea.

blocks.title: Leading hypothesis for Chiari II malformation
steps: Caudal neuropore fails: open lumbosacral myelomeningocele
CSF escapes through the open spinal defect
Ventricles stay undistended; posterior fossa fails to enlarge
Growing hindbrain herniates through the foramen magnum
Fourth ventricle outflow blocked; hydrocephalus develops
blocks.caption: CSF lost through the open defect cannot distend the developing posterior fossa.

blocks.text: Dandy-Walker malformation is the opposite in fossa size. The vermis is absent or hypoplastic, especially its inferior part, the fourth ventricle is dilated into a large cyst filling an enlarged posterior fossa, and the tentorium and confluence of sinuses are displaced upward. It is thought to arise from abnormal development of the roof of the rhombencephalon, with delayed or failed opening of the fourth ventricle outflow. Most patients develop hydrocephalus and present in infancy with an enlarging head and prominent occiput; ataxia and developmental delay vary, and agenesis of the corpus callosum often coexists.

blocks.predict: An adult has wasting of the hand muscles and lost pain and temperature over both shoulders, with normal vibration sense. Which malformation, and which fibers fail first?
blocks.explain: Chiari I with a cervical syrinx. The cavity first cuts spinothalamic fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure, sparing the dorsal columns, then reaches the anterior horns.
blocks.check: The Chiari I and syrinx paragraphs.

integration.text: Neural tube development links biochemistry, signaling, and cell biology. Folate one-carbon chemistry supplies thymidylate and purines for the dividing neural folds, so maternal folate status at conception, MTHFR variants, and drugs that interfere with folate, such as valproate, alter the risk of open defects. SHH, which depends on cholesterol, divides the forebrain and the face together, which is why trisomy 13, Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, and Smoothened blockade all produce holoprosencephaly with midline facial defects. Cell origin predicts where disease appears: crest tumors and migration failures (neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, melanoma, Hirschsprung disease) arise outside the CNS, oligodendrocyte disease spares peripheral nerve, Schwann cell disease spares the brain, and mesodermal microglia are the CNS cells HIV infects.

Anatomy and pathology connect these steps to findings. The ventricles are the persistent lumen of the tube, so hydrocephalus is localized by which ventricles dilate, and the posterior fossa malformations are separated by fossa size and CSF flow. There are limits: MSAFP is a screening probability affected by dating, twins, and abdominal wall defects; the hydrodynamic explanations for Chiari II and for syrinx formation are well supported but not proven; and thresholds such as the 5 mm tonsillar descent are imaging conventions rather than sharp biological boundaries.

summary: Notochord and prechordal mesoderm block BMP4 with noggin, chordin, and follistatin, so the overlying ectoderm becomes the neural plate in week 3.
Neural folds fuse first in the future cervical region and close toward both ends; the cranial neuropore closes about day 25 and the caudal about day 28.
Three primary vesicles become five secondary vesicles, and each lumen persists as a ventricle: lateral (telencephalon), third (diencephalon), aqueduct (mesencephalon), fourth (rhombencephalon).
Retina, optic nerve, posterior pituitary, and pineal are diencephalic outgrowths; the anterior pituitary is oral ectoderm.
Neuroectoderm forms CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependyma; neural crest forms peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, and melanocytes; microglia are mesodermal.
Open defects (myelomeningocele, anencephaly) raise amniotic and maternal AFP and amniotic acetylcholinesterase; skin-covered defects do not.
Folate supplies one-carbon units for thymidylate and purine synthesis in the rapidly dividing neural folds, so maternal folate status at conception sets risk.
Holoprosencephaly is failed forebrain division from defective SHH midline signaling (SHH mutation, trisomy 13, cholesterol synthesis defects), and the face parallels the brain.
Chiari I is tonsillar descent with a small fossa and syringomyelia; Chiari II is vermis and medulla descent with myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus.
Dandy-Walker is vermis agenesis with a cystic fourth ventricle in an enlarged posterior fossa, usually with hydrocephalus.

verify: Neuropore closure days are given as about day 25 (cranial) and about day 28 (caudal) following Langman; some texts give ranges of 24 to 26 and 26 to 28 days.
Timing of forebrain division is given as about weeks 5 to 6; some sources place the critical period at the end of week 4.
Microglia are stated to arise from yolk sac macrophage progenitors (mesoderm), the current consensus; older texts cite bone marrow monocytes. Confirm the expected answer is mesoderm.

Origin of the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid) is given as neural crest in Langman for the cranial region but mesoderm elsewhere; it was left out of the derivatives table for that reason. Parafollicular C cells, classically taught as neural crest, are of endodermal origin in recent lineage studies; confirm the expected answer before adding them.
The Chiari I threshold (at least about 5 mm of tonsillar descent) and the proportion of patients with syringomyelia vary between sources.
MSAFP cutoff (about 2.0 to 2.5 MoM) and screening window (about 15 to 20 weeks) vary by laboratory and guideline.
Folic acid doses for prevention are a Part II management topic and are not stated here; confirm NABNE does not expect them in Part I.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Arnold-Chiari and foramen of Monro, Magendie, and Luschka, and the prenatal lemon and banana signs of Chiari II (omitted here).
